title: Freight Cost Management for Suppliers
summary: Freight cost management starts with four layers: base rate, fuel, fees, and retailer terms. See which ones suppliers can influence this quarter.
body_markdown:
# Freight Cost Management for Suppliers


By[Victoria London](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/profile/victoria-london) , *Content Writer*


Last Updated November 17, 2026


8 min read


In this article, learn about:


-


What freight cost management means for a supplier selling into retail


-


How this cycle’s carrier, fuel, and truckload increases reach a supplier’s freight bill


-


The four layers of a freight bill and which ones a supplier can influence


-


How prepaid and collect terms change who absorbs a rate increase


Freight cost management is the practice of tracking, analyzing, and controlling what it costs to move goods from a supplier to a customer. For a supplier selling into retail, it covers the charges carriers bill, such as base rates, fuel surcharges, and accessorial fees, and it also covers the terms and penalties that retailers attach to each shipment.


The work is getting harder this quarter because several increases are arriving at once. The Cass Freight Index reported that[total freight spending rose 20.4% year over year in September](https://www.thetrucker.com/trucking-news/business/cass-freight-index-freight-shipments-grow-for-a-second-month) , and Cass expects October spending to rise about 23% if normal seasonal patterns hold.


But a market-wide number does not show what reaches supplier profit margins, because the same increase lands differently on a prepaid supplier, a collect supplier, and a supplier that also carries a retailer penalty.


This article breaks the freight bill into four layers so that operations and finance teams can see which ones they can influence before the carrier increases take effect in December and January.


## Why Are Freight Costs Rising Again This Quarter?


### What Do the Latest Freight Numbers Show?


Cass reports that shipments rose 1.9% year over year in September and that its truckload linehaul index rose 10.1%, while higher volumes, rates, and fuel surcharges together pushed total freight spending up 20.4%, a reading the[Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) series for Cass expenditures](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/?graph_id=718411) also shows.


Diesel adds to the picture: The Energy Information Administration (EIA) put the U.S. on-highway diesel average at[$6.352 per gallon for the week of Oct. 26](https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/gasdiesel/?hl=en) , which is $2.634 higher than a year earlier. These market figures come from outside SPS, so they show the direction of costs rather than what any one supplier pays.


### How Are UPS and FedEx Raising Rates and Freight Surcharges?


Both carriers announced an average increase of 5.9%, but their effective dates differ, and each makes changes beyond the average.


**Carrier**


**Effective Date**


**Average Increase**


**Other Changes Taking Effect**


UPS


Dec. 21, 2026


5.9%


Changes to area-surcharge ZIP codes and zone alignment, and a higher minimum billable weight (40 to 50 pounds) for additional-handling packages


FedEx


Jan. 4, 2027


5.9%


Higher minimum rates and surcharges on the same date, such as the commercial delivery area surcharge rising from $4.45 to $4.70


Averages hide a lot of variation. Loop’s head of parcel contract intelligence cautioned that[UPS’s 5.9% is an average on base rates](https://supplychaindive.com/news/ups-plans-59-rate-increase-on-dec-21/872751) that will not match any one shipper’s actual cost, and UPS said on Oct. 26 that more detailed rate previews would come later. Loop’s analysis of FedEx found that[five of its seven major services will rise by more than the average](https://supplychaindive.com/news/fedex-preps-59-rate-hike-surcharge-increases-for-2027/830903) , and that Ground packages between one and five pounds will rise 6.49%.


**Related Reading:**[2026 Freight Market Outlook: Costs, Capacity & Strategy](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/2026-freight-market-outlook/) **


## What Are the Four Layers of a Freight Bill?


A freight bill combines charges from several different sources, and separating them shows where a supplier has real leverage.


**Layer**


**Who Sets It**


**Can a Supplier Influence It?**


Base rate


The carrier, through its rate increase and the supplier’s contract


Partly, through contract rates, caps, and accurate shipment dimensions


Fuel


The carrier, through a surcharge that follows diesel prices


Rarely, other than through contract language


Accessorial and surcharge fees


The carrier, such as delivery area and handling fees


Partly, through packaging and how shipments are described


Retailer terms


The retailer, through its routing guide and compliance program


Not the terms themselves, but largely yes for documentation and on-time performance


The first three layers come from the carrier, so a supplier’s influence over them runs through contract terms and shipment data. The fourth layer comes from the retailer and depends largely on the supplier’s own documentation and on-time performance.


## Who Absorbs the Increase Under Prepaid vs Collect Freight?


The two terms spread an increase across the supply chain in different ways.


### What Happens Under Prepaid Terms?


Under prepaid terms, the supplier is responsible for the shipment until it reaches the retailer’s distribution center or store. According to The Supply Chain Source’s guide to inbound freight, the supplier picks the carrier, negotiates rates, and schedules routing, and it usually builds those costs into the price of its goods.


A carrier increase therefore reaches the supplier directly, and unless the supplier can reprice, it absorbs the higher base rate, fuel charges, and fees while also owning accountability for arrival windows.


### What Happens Under Collect Terms?


Under collect terms, the retailer chooses the carrier and pays the freight bill, so the increase does not appear on the supplier’s own carrier invoices, although it can still reach the supplier indirectly. The same guide describes a freight factor, which Walmart typically applies by requiring a lower-cost quote from the supplier, so the supplier ends up paying for freight through reduced margin.


Walmart’s Collect Pickup Program also adds pickup charges and fuel surcharges that are deducted directly from supplier invoices, which means collect terms change the form of an increase more than they remove it.


**Related Reading:**[Inbound Freight for New Suppliers: LTL, FTL, and Collect vs. Prepaid](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/inbound-freight-for-new-suppliers-ltl-ftl-and-collect-vs-prepaid) **


## What Does One Order Look Like Before and After an Increase?


The example below is illustrative. It applies the 5.9% average increase to a $50.00 base rate that stands in for a supplier’s own number, and it uses FedEx’s published delivery area surcharge amounts for commercial addresses. Fuel is left out because it moves with diesel prices.


**Line Item**


**Before**


**After**


**Change**


Base rate (illustrative)


$50.00


$52.95


+$2.95


Delivery area surcharge, commercial (FedEx published)


$4.45


$4.70


+$0.25


Order freight total, excluding fuel


$54.45


$57.65


+$3.20


On this order, a prepaid supplier would carry an extra $3.20 unless it reprices, and the same arithmetic repeats on every comparable order the supplier ships. The retailer-terms layer sits outside the table because penalty amounts depend on each retailer’s rules, and a supplier’s own freight costs will give a more accurate picture than this example.


## How Do Retailer Routing Guide Penalties Stack on Top of Freight?


Penalties tie most closely to a supplier’s own operations, and they add to the freight bill instead of replacing any part of it. The Supply Chain Source’s inbound freight guide points to three common sources.


Late arrivals under prepaid terms: Under Walmart’s current on-time, in-full (OTIF) targets, as the guide describes them, prepaid suppliers have a 90% on-time goal, and if the carrier misses the Must Arrive By Date window, the fine goes to the supplier. Collect suppliers have a 98% Collect Ready goal and are not responsible for when the truck arrives.


Documentation errors: A missing advance ship notice (ASN) or an inaccurate bill of lading (BOL) can trigger receiving deductions, and a barcode that does not match the ASN may fail to scan in an automated distribution center. The cost of the resulting manual handling is almost always passed back to the supplier.


Freight class and shipment dimensions: In 2025, the National Motor Freight Traffic Association moved nearly 2,000 commodities to density-based freight classes, so accurate dimensions on the BOL now matter more for avoiding reclassification fees on less-than-truckload (LTL) shipments.


Penalty amounts vary by retailer, and each retailer’s routing guide lists its own amounts.


## What Should You Check This Quarter?


A margin check for the next two quarters can follow these steps:


1.


Pull the last 90 days of freight invoices and sort each charge into base rate, fuel, accessorial fees, or retailer-terms charges, so that each layer has its own total.


2.


Read carrier contracts for rate caps and fuel surcharge language, then compare them with the UPS (Dec. 21) and FedEx (Jan. 4) effective dates.


3.


Compare ASN and BOL accuracy over the same 90 days against receiving deductions and OTIF fines.


4.


Model the increase on two or three representative orders, as in the example above.


5.


Prepare the surcharge or repricing conversation with retailers, using the layer breakdown as support.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is the 5.9% carrier increase what suppliers will actually pay?


No, because both carriers describe 5.9% as an average, and for UPS that average applies to base rates. The actual impact depends on the service used, the package characteristics, and the supplier’s contract, and FedEx Ground packages of one to five pounds are rising 6.49% while surcharges rise separately.


### Does collect shipping protect a supplier from freight inflation?


Not fully. The retailer pays the carrier under collect terms, but the supplier can still pay indirectly through a freight factor and, at Walmart, through Collect Pickup Program charges deducted from invoices.


### When do the carrier increases and new fees take effect?


UPS’s increase begins Dec. 21, 2026, and FedEx’s begins Jan. 4, 2027. FedEx also plans new fees on Jan. 18, including $25 when a trade document is not provided electronically and $5 for U.S. domestic and export shipments started with manual paper airbills.


## Ready To Protect the Layers You Control?


As order complexity and retailer requirements grow, suppliers need stronger operational infrastructure to keep up, and that is where[SPS Fulfillment and electronic data interchange (EDI)](https://www.spscommerce.com/products/fulfillment/edi/) fits in. Accurate purchase orders, ship notices, and invoices, with each retailer’s requirements and changes handled at the network level, help keep avoidable penalties from stacking on top of freight costs.


Not ready for EDI?[The Supply Chain Source](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/) has more freight and compliance guides for suppliers.
